intro: To a computer, text is a row of numbers. Type something and see which bytes it becomes – or write bytes and read the text.

errors.invalidDigit: There is a character here that is not a digit in this format.
errors.incompleteByte: The digits do not make whole bytes: binary needs groups of 8 digits, hex groups of 2.

bytes.utf8Title: How many bytes does a character need?
bytes.utf8Explain: UTF-8 stores every character in 1 to 4 bytes: Latin letters and digits in 1 byte, umlauts and Persian letters in 2, the euro sign in 3, most emoji in 4. That is why a Persian text takes about twice as many bytes as an English one with the same number of letters.
bytes.tableCaption: Each character with its Unicode code point and its UTF-8 bytes
bytes.bitsLegend: Each box is one bit: filled means 1, empty means 0. Eight bits make a byte.

morse.unsupported: There is no Morse code for:
morse.unsupportedNote: International Morse code only knows the 26 Latin letters, é, the digits and a few punctuation marks – no umlauts, no ß and no Persian letters. These characters are left out.
morse.unknown: This sequence is not a Morse character:
morse.speed: Slow speed, five words a minute: about {seconds} seconds.
morse.noAudio: This browser cannot make a sound; the light still works.
morse.timelineNote: A dot lasts one unit, a dash three. Letters are three units apart, words seven.
morse.truth: Morse is an encoding too: each character becomes a pattern of short and long – just as a computer turns each character into a pattern of 0 and 1.
